source_text: Most mathematicians think of set theory as providing the basic foundations for mathematics. So how does this really work? For example, how do we translate the sentence “<MATH_0001> is a scheme” into set theory? Well, we just unravel the definitions: A scheme is a locally ringed space such that every point has an open neighbourhood which is an affine scheme. A locally ringed space is a ringed space such that every stalk of the structure sheaf is a local ring. A ringed space is a pair <MATH_0002> consisting of a topological space <MATH_0003> and a sheaf of rings <MATH_0004> on it. A topological space is a pair <MATH_0005> consisting of a set <MATH_0006> and a set of subsets <MATH_0007> satisfying the axioms of a topology. And so on and so forth.

So how, given a set <MATH_0001> would we recognize whether it is a scheme? The first thing we look for is whether the set <MATH_0002> is an ordered pair. This is defined (see <CITE_0001>, page 7) as saying that <MATH_0003> has the form <MATH_0004> for some sets <MATH_0005>. If this is the case, then we would take a look to see whether <MATH_0006> is an ordered pair <MATH_0007>. If so we would check whether <MATH_0008>, and if so whether <MATH_0009> forms the collection of sets for a topology on the set <MATH_0010>. And so on and so forth.

So even though it would take a considerable amount of work to write a complete formula <MATH_0001> with one free variable <MATH_0002> in set theory that expresses the notion “<MATH_0003> is a scheme”, it is possible to do so. The same thing should be true for any mathematical object.
